source_read: PDF, American Journal of Psychiatry 158: 1206-1214 (all nine pages; native text layer): full text, Table 1, figure legends, funding and affiliation note; Table 1 ages, Kendall's tau p-values (normal approximation) and Hedges' g recomputed from the printed values.

key_findings.note: 'Close to the tracer's non-specific binding' is the card's inference; the paper says only that a tracer with a higher specific-to-nonspecific binding ratio is needed to detect low binding-site density (p. 1211).
Editors' check with n = 11 (normal approximation, no tie correction): tau -0.48 gives p of about 0.04 and -0.73 about 0.002, consistent with the printed thresholds.

key_findings.correction: The discussion's reading of the null correlation, that a lasting reduction could occur, supported by a previous PET study rather than by these data, is on p. 1212 (paragraph beginning 'We found no significant correlation'), not p. 1211. The same page error appears in interpretation_gap (claimed), point 2.

(a) The symptom counts describe the 2 weeks before the PET examination: 3 with persistent psychotic symptoms, 4 with anxiety-like symptoms and 3 with none, plus participant 1, whose psychotic symptoms began during use and were still present on the scan day (7 days abstinent), so 4 of 11 had psychotic symptoms at the scan. (b) The paper says none had a history of psychotic symptoms before methamphetamine use, not that none had any psychiatric history (p. 1208, Results, 1st paragraph).

key_findings.note: The same paragraph goes on to say that people who use methamphetamine may have a greater risk of Parkinson's disease as they age, and that the small reduction appears to predict psychiatric signs; see missed.

reporting_issues.note: The issue stands (df = 10 is a non-standard label), but the consequence should be withdrawn: the p-values can be approximately reconstructed from tau and n = 11. Editors' calculation (normal approximation, no tie correction): tau -0.48 gives p of about 0.04; -0.50, 0.03; -0.62, 0.008; 0.64, 0.006; -0.73, 0.002. All are consistent with the printed thresholds.
Recomputed from Table 1: mean 28.0, SD 5.69 (n - 1 denominator).
Location detail: the paragraph starts on p. 1211 and the quoted phrase ends on p. 1212 (pp. 1211-1212).

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high agreed: confounding and selection of participants are high. ROBINS-E fits the cross-sectional exposure design.

risk_of_bias_domains.note: A further selection effect: people with a history of seizures, dyskinesia or coma, complications the paper links to high-dose intoxication (p. 1207), were excluded, which removes the most severe cases from the methamphetamine group.

Supporting point: the BPRS rater was the first author (Y.S., p. 1207), stated to be blind to the PET data only; blinding to the use histories is not stated, so the positive-symptom versus duration correlation (tau 0.64) is not shown to be rated blind to duration.

ROBINS-E domain 7 asks whether the reported result was selected from several measurements or analyses on the basis of its findings. Here the null results are reported alongside the significant ones: no correlation with abstinence, none for the prefrontal cortex, none between craving and binding or duration of use (p. 1209), and the primary measure (k3/k4) is the one the Methods define. The unreported rate-constant comparisons and the prefrontal 'data not shown' justify some concerns. The 21 uncorrected tests are a multiplicity problem for interpreting the correlations, already recorded under reporting issues, rather than evidence of selective reporting. The overall judgment stays high.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial agreed; the card understates it. The discussion states outright that 'methamphetamine causes reduction of the dopamine transporter density' (p. 1210, Discussion, 1st paragraph), stronger than the abstract's 'may cause'. On p. 1212 it adds that the small caudate/putamen reduction appears to have predictive value for psychiatric signs, and that people who use methamphetamine may have a greater risk of Parkinson's disease as they age, although no one was followed and no one was assessed for Parkinson's disease beyond the exclusion of parkinsonism.

missed: Interpretation statements not on the card: the explicit causal sentence on p. 1210 and the predictive and Parkinson's-risk statements on p. 1212 (see interpretation_gap note).

BPRS rater (p. 1207, Method, 4th paragraph): the rater was the first author, stated to be blind to the PET data only; the card says only 'one trained psychiatrist'. Who collected the use histories is not stated, and blinding to them is not claimed, so the symptom-duration correlation is not shown to be protected by blinding.

Exclusion of people with seizures, dyskinesia or coma (p. 1207, Method, 1st paragraph), complications the authors associate with high-dose intoxication: the methamphetamine group excludes the most severe cases, which bears on how far the 20-33% reductions generalize.

Card corrections outside the key findings: (1) Hedges' g for the nucleus accumbens is 1.65, about 1.6 (d is 1.72); the caudate/putamen (2.39) and prefrontal (1.43) values are right. (2) Funding: the affiliation note (p. 1213) lists Hamamatsu Photonics among three institutions without saying which authors belong to it, so 'three authors' cannot be checked from the PDF. (3) Selective reporting: the non-significant craving correlations are reported, without statistics (p. 1209), so 'reported only where significant' should read 'statistics given only where significant'. (4) Outcomes: the paper says the MRI images were referred to as anatomical landmarks (p. 1207), not that they were co-registered; and 'This procedure was performed blind to the clinical data' closes the paragraph that begins with the manual region drawing, so it plausibly covers the drawing too.
